notes: **أَلُو is the "hello" used only on the phone.** It isn't used face to face. Then the caller identifies himself: مَعَكَ... ("with you is ...") or أَنَا... Giving your own name first is considered polite and saves time.
**كَيْفَ أَسْتَطِيعُ مُسَاعَدَتَكَ؟** is the standard phrase of office staff. Notice that مُسَاعَدَة ("help") is the noun from سَاعَدَ, and with the ending ـكَ it becomes "helping you".
**لَحْظَةً — "one moment".** Tanwin fathah again, as an adverb. Other equally common forms: ثَانِيَةً (one second), دَقِيقَةً (one minute), لَحْظَةً مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (one moment, please).

**أَسْأَلُ عَنْ — each verb demands its own preposition.** "Ask **about**". Just as in English, each verb has a partner preposition that can't be swapped: يَبْحَثُ عَنْ (look for), يَتَكَلَّمُ عَنْ (talk about), يَشْكُرُ عَلَى (thank for), يَحْتَاجُ إِلَى (need).

**اَلْقَاعَةُ الْكُبْرَى — the feminine "-est" form.** The pattern أَكْبَر has a feminine partner كُبْرَى, used when it follows a definite feminine noun. Others: اَلصُّغْرَى (smallest), اَلْأُولَى (first), اَلْعُلْيَا (highest).
**لَمْ أَسْمَعْ is far more polite than repeating the question.** "I didn't hear well" puts the cause on you, not on how the other person speaks. It's exactly the same courtesy as in English.
**تَمَامٌ means "all good, perfect".** One of the words you'll hear most in Egypt. In the Levant: مَنِيح, and تَمَام is used too. The formal form: حَسَنًا.

grammars.title: Phone phrases from start to finish
after: غَيْرُ means "not, un-" before an adjective: غَيْرُ مَوْجُودٍ (not present), غَيْرُ وَاضِحٍ (unclear), غَيْرُ مُمْكِنٍ (impossible). It complements لَيْسَ for more compact sentences.

grammars.title: Apologizing and thanking
after: جَزَاكَ اللهُ خَيْرًا is widely used by Muslims around the world as "jazakallah khairan", with exactly the same meaning. To a woman: جَزَاكِ اللهُ خَيْرًا; to several people: جَزَاكُمُ اللهُ خَيْرًا.

blocks.text: A short message in Arabic follows three fixed layers: **greeting**, **content**, **closing**. Skipping the greeting feels much ruder than in English — even in the shortest work message.

blocks.title: A complete sample message
items: اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ يَا أُسْتَاذ. أَنَا بُودِي مِنَ الْمُسْتَوَى الثَّانِي. أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَسْأَلَ عَنْ مَوْعِدِ الِامْتِحَانِ. هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ نَلْتَقِيَ غَدًا بَعْدَ الدَّرْسِ؟ شُكْرًا مُقَدَّمًا. مَعَ التَّحِيَّةِ، بُودِي.
Four sentences, all built from material you've had since unit 16. There's no new grammar in it at all — only the arrangement is new.

blocks.text: Notice that many everyday phrases are blessings, and almost all have a **matching reply** — not a repetition. مَبْرُوك is answered with اَللهُ يُبَارِكُ فِيكَ; شُكْرًا with اَلْعَفْوُ; سَلَامَتُكَ with اَللهُ يُسَلِّمُكَ. Learning the pairs is more useful than learning the phrases on their own.
